passages: [prose] Sedentary habitat specialist species were often associated with forest habitats (Tables 2 and S6), including the Northern Chequered Skipper (Carterocephalus silvicola), Clouded Apollo (Parnassius mnemosyne) and Purple Emperor (Apatura ilia). Although several species within this group were associated with semi-natural grassland, including some species of high conservation concern, for example silver-spotted skipper (Hesperia comma), population trajectories for this group are likely to have been strongly influenced by historical forest management practices. During the 20th century, deciduous woodlands of lowland temperate Europe have become increasingly dense and shady due to the replacement of millennia-old management techniques by even-aged tall forest stands, with deleterious impacts for butterflies (Warren & Key, 1991; Bergman & Kindvall, 2004; Spitzer et al., 2008). Furthermore, species-rich ecotones marking the transition zone between closed and open vegetation, and which often harbour high species diversity, including many forest butterflies, have increasingly been replaced by sharp borders. This has had detrimental effects on butterflies such as Ilex Hairstreak (Satyrium ilicis) (Maes et al., 2014). Species marked with '*' have gone extinct in Denmark.

[prose] Results We document severe declines in butterfly diversity over the last century, with substantial regional-scale extinctions leading to a net loss of 10% of all Danish butterfly species. Segregating species into functional groups showed that the highest rate of regional extinction occurred among sedentary habitat specialists overwintering in the egg stage, while the most severe local-scale declines occurred among sedentary host plant specialists overwintering in the larval stage. In contrast, mobile generalist species with mature overwintering stages showed stable richness trends throughout the century. However, a pervasive spatio-temporal biotic homogenization of butterfly assemblages was revealed for all functional groups.

[prose] Our analysis showed that butterfly species could be segregated into three clearly separated functional groups, which showed marked differences in the strength, timing and spatial scale of richness change. The highest rate of regional extinction occurred among sedentary habitat specialists overwintering in the egg stage (cluster 2), while the most severe local-scale losses occurred among sedentary host plant specialists overwintering in the larval stage (cluster 1). In contrast, mobile species with broad ecological adaptations and mature overwintering stages (cluster 3) were stable throughout the century.
